title: Human Spatial Behavior
review_question: To critically evaluate past approaches and recent developments in the field of human spatial behavior, emphasizing theoretical drifts and the need for sociological input.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: The review focuses on work related to social and psychological variables in association with the spatial dimension, covering interpersonal distancing, small-group ecology, and crowding. It implicitly excludes more technically oriented disciplines.

findings.antecedent: Abnormal spatial situations (e.g., very close individual distances, territorial invasions, overcrowded conditions)
findings.consequent: Heightened physiological arousal
findings.quote: Several studies in fact found a relationship between spatial circumstances and heightened arousal as measured by self-reports and machines

findings.antecedent: Abnormal spatial situations (e.g., close individual distances, territorial invasions, overcrowded conditions)
findings.consequent: Specific kinds of overt behavioral responses (e.g., aggression, abnormal behavior, psychological stress)
findings.quote: There is no consistent evidence, however, that abnormal spatial situations elicit specific kinds of responses among humans.

findings.antecedent: Infringement upon a person's spatial domain by an experimental confederate
findings.consequent: Behavioral response
findings.quote: When a person's spatial domain is infringed upon by an experimental confederate... the response is typically to flee and rarely to take the expected aggressive stance.

findings.antecedent: Spatial zones occupied by ongoing groups
findings.consequent: Avoidance of use of those zones by others
findings.quote: people will avoid the use of spatial zones that are occupied by ongoing groups.

findings.antecedent: Different cultures (e.g., 'contact cultures' vs. 'noncontact cultures')
findings.consequent: Interpersonal distances and densities considered appropriate
findings.quote: persons from different cultures vary in the interpersonal distances and densities that they consider to be appropriate.

findings.antecedent: Subcultural groups within the United States (e.g., Spanish-surnamed, blacks)
findings.consequent: Spatial preferences (interpersonal distances)
findings.quote: Spanish-surnamed groups interact at closer distances than whites... but no consistent findings emerged from studies of blacks

findings.antecedent: Cultural training (e.g., values, educators rewarding/punishing spatial choices)
findings.consequent: Individual adjustment of personal distances
findings.quote: individuals adjust their personal distances on the basis of new contingencies.

findings.antecedent: Physical characteristics of a setting (e.g., building design, furniture arrangement)
findings.consequent: Human attitudes and actions (e.g., social interaction, group formation)
findings.quote: while design may facilitate or inhibit action, it does not determine behavior

findings.antecedent: Design factors that foster perceived domain of residents and community surveillance in public housing
findings.consequent: Crime rates
findings.quote: differential rates of crime in urban public housing could be explained by design factors.

findings.antecedent: Forced spatial proximity (e.g., due to low-rise, high-density design, shared community facilities)
findings.consequent: Social interaction and community spirit (cooperation, communality)
findings.quote: design can force spatial proximity, and this inevitably leads to social interaction and community spirit.

findings.antecedent: Sociopetal furniture arrangements (e.g., diagonal seating)
findings.consequent: Long, comfortable, physically close interactions and group formation
findings.quote: certain arrangements of chairs would be conducive to long, comfortable, physically close interactions

findings.antecedent: Room designs and imagined ongoing activity
findings.consequent: Perceptions of crowding (what is considered overcrowded)
findings.quote: Not only did individuals vary the densities with room designs but, importantly, also with the imagined ongoing activity.

findings.antecedent: Perceived crowding (subjective feeling of spatial inadequacy)
findings.consequent: Poorer academic performance and health
findings.quote: perceived crowding was related to poorer academic performance and health among university students.

findings.antecedent: Objective household space (persons per room)
findings.consequent: Perceived crowding
findings.quote: only a moderate amount of the variance seems to be explained by objective household space... which indicates that objective density is only part of the spatial problem

findings.antecedent: Perceived household crowding
findings.consequent: Housing satisfaction and preferred mobility
findings.quote: perceived household crowding has an independent effect on measures of housing satisfaction... including an impact on preferred mobility

findings.antecedent: Type of environment (primary vs. secondary, important vs. inconsequential) and source of interference (neutral vs. personal/intentional/unintentional) in a crowded setting
findings.consequent: Human responses and observable stress
findings.quote: the type of environment in which crowding is perceived... and the source of interference... will have a great impact on human responses and observable stress.

findings.antecedent: High density
findings.consequent: Good events better and bad events worse (density-intensity theory)
findings.quote: high density makes good events better and bad events worse, acting as an enhancer.

findings.antecedent: Urban life / high population density (too many daily contacts at close distances)
findings.consequent: Overloading the nervous system / cognitive fatigue
findings.quote: urban life as a situation in which individuals typically had too many daily contacts at very close distances with others. Too many people within an individual's sensory range potentially led to 'overloading' the nervous system.

findings.antecedent: Overstimulation from high density
findings.consequent: Coping responses (e.g., social withdrawal, limiting involvement, avoiding others)
findings.quote: The principal adaptations were referred to as 'social withdrawal,' or attempts by individuals to limit their involvement in some associations and totally avoid others.

findings.antecedent: Decrease in number of visible social stimuli (e.g., by partitions)
findings.consequent: Increased room density (without adverse psychological effects)
findings.quote: room density may be increased (with no adverse psychological effects) when the number of visible social stimuli decrease.

findings.antecedent: High densities
findings.consequent: Learning a strategy of 'specialized withdrawal' (conserving energies by attending to rewarding encounters and avoiding neutral/harmful interactions)
findings.quote: when confronted with high densities, individuals learn to conserve energies by attending to more rewarding encounters and avoiding neutral or potentially harmful interactions.

findings.antecedent: Residential crowding
findings.consequent: Withdrawal from primary relationships (friends, social networks, family, organizations)
findings.quote: individuals experiencing residential crowding do not withdraw from primary relationships

findings.antecedent: Residential crowding
findings.consequent: Involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature (strangers, neighboring, meeting new people)
findings.quote: they seem to decrease involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature

findings.antecedent: Lack of predictability and controllability of environmental stressors (e.g., noise)
findings.consequent: Stress response and aftereffects (e.g., decreased abilities in completing puzzles)
findings.quote: it was the lack of predictability and controllability of the experience that caused a stress response

findings.antecedent: Mere perception of control over an environmental stimulus (e.g., noise, without actual control)
findings.consequent: Behavioral responses to the situation (mitigated stress)
findings.quote: the mere perception of control over the noise stimulus... exerted a significant influence over behavioral responses to the situation.

findings.antecedent: Crowding (situation beyond individual control)
findings.consequent: Poor task performance (aftereffects of stress exposure)
findings.quote: Sherrod (1974) manipulated perceived control in a crowding experiment... and found that the aftereffects of stress exposure... were present in the group that lacked a sense of control over the crowded situation.

findings.antecedent: Chronic household crowding
findings.consequent: Task deficits among children
findings.quote: A field study found that chronic household crowding created task deficits among children

findings.antecedent: Experiencing poor environmental control (e.g., crowding)
findings.consequent: Attitude of powerlessness / 'learned helplessness'
findings.quote: experiencing poor environmental control... leads to an attitude of powerlessness; the result is 'learned helplessness'

findings.antecedent: Amount of control individuals were given during group tasks
findings.consequent: Perceptions of crowding
findings.quote: perceptions of crowding were also affected by the amount of control individuals were given during group tasks

findings.antecedent: Low social power (e.g., urban poor, child in crowded household)
findings.consequent: Claim to space when it is in high demand
findings.quote: people of low status... may have less of a claim to space when it is in high demand

findings.antecedent: Stable, status-differentiated group experiencing a shortage of space (e.g., families in a crowded home)
findings.consequent: Control over space use and activities in its territory (e.g., scheduling activities, regulating space utilization)
findings.quote: A common response of a stable, status-differentiated group experiencing a shortage of space is greater control over space use and activities in its territory.

findings.antecedent: Social meanings that people attach to environments (through interactions and ongoing socialization)
findings.consequent: Human spatial responses
findings.quote: The social meanings that people attach to environments through their interactions and ongoing socialization thus would play an important role in determining human spatial responses

findings.antecedent: Imagery people have of the spaces they use (fantasy vs. reality)
findings.consequent: Coping with existing circumstances and imagining themselves in better positions
findings.quote: people develop these images in order to cope with the existing circumstances and imagine themselves in better positions.

findings.antecedent: Role differentiation
findings.consequent: Spatial differentiation within territories and mechanisms for controlling movement across boundaries (to achieve privacy while allowing access)
findings.quote: role differentiation demands some degree of spatial differentiation within territories... and a mechanism for controlling movement across boundaries.

findings.antecedent: Disagreement on how common space should be allocated (for role enactments)
findings.consequent: Interpersonal tension and role interference
findings.quote: Problems arise when those sharing a common space do not have the same views about how this resource should be allocated, since this could hinder the enactment of individually preferred roles.

findings.antecedent: Short supply of household space / not enough room or privacy
findings.consequent: Role conflict, competition for space use, incomplete role performances, intrusions, blocking of desired role enactments
findings.quote: If there is not enough room or privacy to conduct desired roles alone and with others, competition for space use may occur.

findings.antecedent: Alteration of one factor in interpersonal interaction (e.g., closer distances)
findings.consequent: Shifts along another dimension (e.g., less eye contact) to maintain optimal distance/situational meaning
findings.quote: the alteration of one factor seemed to create shifts along another dimension... to decrease the stress felt from the inappropriateness of the situation.

findings.antecedent: Lack of needed privacy (personal space violations, territorial invasions, crowding) OR inadequate social contact (low density, far interpersonal distances, lack of territorial encroachments)
findings.consequent: Feelings of isolation / unpleasantness
findings.quote: when the needed privacy is lacking... as there are situations in which inadequate social contact leads to feelings of isolation... which can be equally unpleasant.

findings.antecedent: Individuals and groups
findings.consequent: Control over the flow of information across a 'boundary' (to regulate social contacts and attain optimal stimulation)
findings.quote: Altman (1975) thus sees individuals and groups as controlling the flow of information across a 'boundary'... to regulate social contacts in an attempt to attain optimal stimulation.

findings.antecedent: Crowding
findings.consequent: Stress, which sets off a chain reaction (behaviors, attitudes, environmental manipulations) leading to adaptation/successful functioning OR continued stress/malfunctioning
findings.quote: crowding leads to stress, which then sets off a chain reaction... The result is either adaptation and successful functioning... or continued stress and malfunctioning

findings.antecedent: Congruence / close fit between people's needs and their environments
findings.consequent: Functioning in their setting / attaining larger goals
findings.quote: The idea of 'congruence,' or a close fit between people's needs and their environments, has been stressed by a variety of researchers.

findings.antecedent: Spatial circumstances that are incompatible with present needs
findings.consequent: Residential dissatisfaction
findings.quote: the issue thus becomes one of examining the fate of those who are forced to reside in spatial circumstances that are incompatible with their present needs.

synthesis_conclusions: There is an obvious need for further sociological input in the study of human spatial behavior.
Human groups are highly organized, complex social systems that place individuals in unique roles, which has implications for spatial differentiation and control.
Space has objective value as a resource (like time or money) and is subject to cherishing, denial, and competition.
Spatial behavior and uses have important communicative roles in social life, informing individuals of expectations and relationships.
Sociology should actively observe regularities in human reactions to spatial circumstances.
evidence_gaps: Most studies have not considered spatial differentiation, the ordering of activities, or the control of space through social mechanisms.
Most researchers have failed to consider the full range of manipulations of social and spatial variables to optimize rewards.
Studies of socialization of space use and the development of spatial meanings and subsequent responses are lacking.
Surprisingly little work has occurred on the 'antecedent variables' of spatial factors and behaviors.
Sociological methods, such as systematic large-scale surveys and observations conducted over time, are in short supply and high demand.

moderators.effect: Influences appropriate interpersonal distances and densities, though subcultural differences show mixed findings.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Contact cultures prefer smaller distances; Spanish-surnamed groups interact closer than whites, but findings for blacks are inconsistent.

moderators.effect: Individuals with low social power may have less claim to space in high demand, influencing their ability to control their environment.
moderators.subgroup_effects: The urban poor and children in crowded households may experience less control over space.

moderators.effect: Mediates the impact of environmental stressors like noise and crowding, reducing stress responses and task deficits.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Mere perception of control can mitigate stress, and lack of control leads to learned helplessness.

moderators.effect: Influences withdrawal responses to crowding; individuals may withdraw from secondary relationships but not primary ones.
moderators.subgroup_effects: Residential crowding leads to decreased involvement in encounters with strangers/neighbors but not friends/family.

moderators.effect: Females tend to respond more positively to crowded conditions than males.

limitations: Early research was often exploratory and atheoretical, lacking theoretical orientation and interest in improving understanding of the social order.
The field has been characterized by deterministic views and solitary, single-variable experimental studies, which are now recognized as insufficient.
Past models of stimulus overload underestimated human learning and response capabilities and ignored social differences among potential contacts.
The idea that manipulating perceived control alone can 'better' long-term crowded residential environments is considered untested and sociologically naive.
The notion that a general personality attribute of helplessness develops merely from crowded environments is dubious.
Most 'control' studies focus on attitudes, short-term experiences, or special groups, diverting attention from larger sociological structural issues.
The study of roles and symbolic spatial meanings has suffered from little empirical confirmation despite encouraging theorizing.
Equilibrium theories can be misleading if they assume all spatial problems are alleviated or result in balanced solutions, potentially masking ongoing discomfort.
Equilibrium models conspicuously miss notions of social position and antecedent conditions leading to spatial configurations and individual placement.
